title: Del Sol Food Truck
format: Text Narrative  |  Difficulty: 2.5/10  |  (previously Task 21 (orig. Tasks 21–30 set))
narrative:
Two friends grabbed lunch separately from the same food truck, which sells only tacos and burritos at a fixed price each. Ana ordered 4
tacos and 3 burritos and paid $32.00 in total. Ben ordered 2 tacos and 5 burritos — and when he compared receipts with Ana afterward,
he realized he had paid exactly $5.00 more than she did, even though neither of them knew the other's order size in advance.
given:
Nothing here states the taco or burrito price directly. What is known is Ana's order and total, plus a comparison between Ben's total and
Ana's — that comparison must first be turned into an actual dollar figure for Ben's order before a system of two equations can be written.
statements: Ben paid more for his 5 burritos alone than Ana paid for her entire order.
A burrito costs $2.50 more than a taco.
Had Ana ordered one fewer burrito (4 tacos and 2 burritos instead), she would have paid less than $28.00.
Ben's total order price exceeds $40.00.
Buying 6 tacos and 6 burritos together would cost $57.00.
explanations: Ben's 5 burritos alone cost 5 × 6.00 = $30.00, less than Ana's full $32.00 order, not more. It's tempting to assume the person who 'paid more overall' also wins every partial comparison, but that isn't guaranteed here.
6.00 − 3.50 = $2.50 exactly, matching the solved prices.
4 tacos and 2 burritos would cost 4(3.50) + 2(6.00) = $26.00, indeed under $28.00.
Ben's order was built to total exactly $37.00, which does not exceed $40.00. Forgetting the $5.00 gap was already used to build the model — and adding it again on top of $37 — is a common slip.
6 tacos and 6 burritos cost 6(3.50) + 6(6.00) = $57.00 exactly.
solution:
Multiply the second equation by 2: 4x + 10y = 74.00. Subtract the first (4x + 3y = 32.00): 7y = 42.00, so y = 6.00. Substituting back: 4x +
18.00 = 32.00 → x = 3.50.
Final Answer: Taco = $3.50  |  Burrito = $6.00
general: The whole task rests on one small translation step: converting "Ben paid $5.00 more than Ana" into the equation 2x + 5y = 37.00. Once that is done, it is a completely ordinary elimination with round-number answers. Statement A is the main conceptual trap, testing whether "paid more overall" is wrongly assumed to extend to every partial sub-comparison.

title: Northgate Books Monthly Sales Report
format: Sales Report + Memo  |  Difficulty: 2.7/10  |  (previously Task 22 (orig. Tasks 21–30 set))
narrative:
Metric
Value
Paperback units sold
400
Hardcover units sold
220
Combined revenue (paperback + hardcover)
$8,540
Full-time staff on payroll
12
Loyalty-member share of purchases
45%
Memo — Pricing Desk: "Hardcover editions are priced exactly $5 above the paperback price this quarter, across the board."
given:
Let x = paperback price, y = hardcover price. Staff headcount and the loyalty-member percentage do not affect unit pricing and should be
set aside.
statements: A paperback price of $12 is consistent with the pricing desk's $5 gap rule.
Hardcover editions are priced above $18.
Had 500 paperbacks been sold instead of 400 (hardcover sales unchanged), revenue would have been $1,200 higher.
A customer buying 3 hardcovers and 2 paperbacks would pay less than $75.
The reported $8,540 total could also have come from selling 310 hardcovers alone.
explanations: With x = 12, the memo's rule gives y = 17, an exact $5 gap, so the two pieces of information are consistent.
The hardcover price settles at exactly $17.00, not above $18. Assuming a 'clean' $20 hardcover price without solving the system is a typical shortcut.
100 extra paperbacks at $12 each adds exactly $1,200, using only the paperback price and the change in quantity.
3 hardcovers and 2 paperbacks cost 3(17) + 2(12) = $75.00 exactly — equal to, not less than, $75.
310 hardcovers alone would bring in 310 × 17 = $5,270, nowhere near $8,540. The staff and loyalty-share figures are irrelevant distractions.
solution:
Substitute directly: 400x + 220(x + 5) = 8540. Expanding: 620x + 1100 = 8540 → 620x = 7440 → x = 12. Then y = 12 + 5 = 17.
Final Answer: Paperback = $12.00  |  Hardcover = $17.00
general: A relation-plus-total system solved in one substitution step, with two deliberately irrelevant operational figures (headcount, loyalty share) planted in the report. Statement D is a boundary trap ('less than' vs. 'equal to'), and statement E tests whether decoy data gets mistakenly folded into the calculation.

title: SkyLink Mobile Promotional Flyer
format: Promotional Flyer  |  Difficulty: 2.8/10  |  (previously Task 25 (orig. Tasks 21–30 set))
narrative:
SKYLINK MOBILE: BASIC — $15/month base + $2.00/GB overage. STANDARD — base fee and overage rate confirmed by billing history
below. PREMIUM — $40/month, unlimited, no overage.
Month
Overage Used
Total Bill
March
8 GB
$62.00
April
3 GB
$47.00
given:
Let x = Standard plan's base fee, y = its per-GB overage rate. The Basic and Premium prices belong to different plans and should not be
substituted into this customer's equations.
statements: The Standard plan has a lower base fee than the advertised Basic plan.
The overage rate on the Standard plan is $3.00 per GB.
A Standard customer using 10 GB of overage in May would be billed $68.00.
Switching from Standard to Premium would save money for a customer who typically uses 5 GB of overage per month.
For a customer using 8 GB of overage, the Basic plan works out cheaper than the Standard plan.
explanations: Standard's base fee is $38.00, well above Basic's $15.00 — the higher figure buys a lower overage rate instead.
The elimination step isolates y = 3 directly, confirmed by both bills.
38 + 10(3) = $68.00 exactly, extending the confirmed rate to a new usage figure.
At 5 GB of overage, Standard costs 38 + 15 = $53.00, versus Premium's flat $40.00 — a $13.00 saving.
At 8 GB, Basic costs 15 + 8(2) = $31.00 versus Standard's 38 + 24 = $62.00 — Basic is substantially cheaper here.
solution:
Subtract directly: 5y = 15, so y = 3. Substitute back: x + 9 = 47, so x = 38.
Final Answer: Standard base fee = $38.00  |  Overage rate = $3.00/GB
general: The simplest possible subtract-directly elimination (matching x-coefficients), dressed up with two decoy competitor plans that must be ignored when building the model but become relevant again for the decision-style statements D and E. Statement A is the main trap, testing whether 'advertised as entry-level' gets wrongly equated with 'cheapest base fee.'

title: Lakeview Inn Booking Confirmations
format: Booking Confirmation  |  Difficulty: 3.0/10  |  (previously Task 23 (orig. Tasks 21–30 set))
narrative:
LAKEVIEW INN — Rate Card. Standard Rooms & Suites, free breakfast & Wi-Fi, all rates subject to 8% occupancy tax.
Confirmation
Standard Rooms
Suites
Total Charged (incl. 8% tax)
Weekend 1
10
4
$2,419.20
Weekend 2
7
9
$3,099.60
given:
Let x = nightly Standard rate, y = nightly Suite rate, both before tax. Each total must first be converted back to a pre-tax figure before it
can be used in the model.
statements: After removing the occupancy tax, Weekend 1's booking revenue was $2,240.00.
A Suite costs $200 more per night than a Standard room.
Booking 6 Standard rooms for one night (pre-tax) costs less than booking 4 Suites.
Including the 8% tax, a single Suite night costs $226.80.
Had Weekend 2 booked 10 Suites instead of 9 (Standard rooms unchanged), pre-tax revenue would have risen by $210.
explanations: 2419.20 ÷ 1.08 = 2240.00 exactly, matching the pre-tax figure used to build the model.
The actual gap is 210 − 140 = $70, not $200. Forgetting to strip out the tax before comparing rates tends to inflate this estimate.
6 Standard rooms cost 6(140) = $840 and 4 Suites cost 4(210) = $840 — exactly equal, not one less than the other.
210 × 1.08 = $226.80, applying the same tax used to convert the confirmations.
One additional Suite adds exactly $210 in pre-tax revenue, since the Standard-room count is unchanged.
solution:
From the first equation, 5x + 2y = 1120, so y = (1120 − 5x)/2. Substituting into the second: 14x + 9(1120 − 5x) = 5740 → −31x = −4340
→ x = 140. Then y = 210.
Final Answer: Standard = $140.00/night (pre-tax)  |  Suite = $210.00/night (pre-tax)
general: Adds a tax-removal division step before the standard elimination, which is a genuinely new mechanism relative to Tasks 11–13. Statement C is a boundary-equality trap, and statement B punishes comparing tax-inclusive figures without adjusting for the 8% markup first.

narrative:

Warehouse floor space: 12,000 sq ft. On-site staff: 9. (Not needed below.)
given:
Only the January and February rows report actual recorded values; March is explicitly labelled a forecast and cannot be used to solve for
today's unit costs.
statements: Component A's unit cost is $12.
Component B's unit cost is $18.
The March forecast assumes higher unit prices than what actually applied in January and February.
If March's forecast quantities (200 A + 100 B) were valued at the actual January/February unit costs, the result would be $4,700.
The combined actual inventory value recorded for January and February is $6,810.
explanations: The elimination confirms x = $12.00 exactly, reconciling with both actual monthly rows.
Component B actually costs $15.00, not $18.00. Reading the forecast row's higher implied prices back into the actual data is a natural but incorrect shortcut.
At actual costs, 200(12) + 100(15) = $3,900, well below the $4,700 forecast — the forecast does build in a price increase.
Valuing March's quantities at actual costs gives $3,900, not $4,700 — the $4,700 figure only appears because the forecast bakes in an assumed price rise.
Simply adding the two actual monthly totals, 3,150 + 3,660 = $6,810, without needing the unit costs at all.
solution:
Divide by 30 and 10 respectively: 5x + 3y = 105; 13x + 14y = 366. Multiply by 14 and 3: 70x + 42y = 1470; 39x + 42y = 1098.
Subtracting: 31x = 372, so x = 12. Then 3y = 45, y = 15.
Final Answer: Component A = $12.00/unit  |  Component B = $15.00/unit
general: Introduces the "identify which rows are real data" mechanism: a third, forecast row must be recognized and excluded before the system is even built. Statements B and D both punish letting the excluded forecast row leak back into the reasoning.

title: Sunrise Staffing, Overtime Contract Check

narrative:
Sunrise Staffing's contract states overtime must be paid at exactly 1.5× the regular hourly wage. A union representative pulled this
week's payroll for two workers, both completing a full 40-hour regular week, to check whether that rule was actually followed.

given:
Let x = regular hourly wage, y = overtime rate actually paid. Only once both rates are known can they be compared against the contract's
1.5× rule.
statements: The overtime rate actually paid matches the contractual 1.5× regular-rate rule.
The regular hourly wage is $14.
Relative to the 1.5× contract rule, Worker 2 was overpaid by exactly $6.00 on their overtime hours.
A third worker completing 40 regular + 4 overtime hours, paid at the rates actually used this week, would earn $656.
That same third worker, paid strictly under the 1.5× contract rule instead, would earn $644.
explanations: 1.5 × $14.00 = $21.00, but the payroll data shows $24.00 was actually paid — the contract's rule was not followed.
The elimination step isolates x = $14.00 directly, and it checks out against both workers' totals.
Under contract, 2 overtime hours should cost 2(21) = $42; the worker was actually paid 2(24) = $48, an overpayment of $6.00.
Using rates actually paid: 40(14) + 4(24) = $656.
Using the contractual rate: 40(14) + 4(21) = $644, $12 less than the company's actual practice.
solution:
Subtracting cancels the 40x term: 4y = 96, so y = 24. Substituting back: 40x + 48 = 608, so x = 14.
Final Answer: Regular wage = $14.00/hr  |  Overtime actually paid = $24.00/hr (contract requires $21.00/hr)
general: A claim-verification task: the algebra is a simple direct-subtract elimination, but every statement requires holding two parallel numbers in mind (what was actually paid vs. what the contract requires) rather than just one solved value.

title: Riverside Water Utility, Billing Dispute
format: Text Narrative  |  Difficulty: 3.4/10  |  (previously Task 26 (orig. Tasks 21–30 set))
narrative:
A customer contacted Riverside Water to query two consecutive bills. She used 18 m³ in May and was billed $56.10 — but May's bill also
carried a 10% late penalty applied to the entire bill. In June she used 25 m³ with no penalty, billed $65.00. The billing office insists its
fixed charge is $18.00 and its rate is $1.85 per m³.
given:
Since the 10% penalty was applied to May's whole bill rather than as a flat add-on, May's reported total must first be divided back down.
The fixed charge and rate must be derived independently from the two bills, since the phone claim may not be accurate.
statements: The billing office's claim of an $18.00 fixed monthly charge is correct.
The rate charged is $2.00 per cubic metre.
After removing the late penalty, May's actual water charge was $51.00.
A customer using 40 m³ in a month would be billed $85.00.
Had the same 10% late penalty been applied to June's $65.00 bill, the total would have been $71.50.
explanations: The bills actually support a fixed charge of $15.00, not the claimed $18.00 — the billing office's own figure is wrong.
The elimination step gives y = $2.00 per m³ exactly, contradicting the claimed $1.85.
56.10 ÷ 1.10 = $51.00, undoing the 10% penalty rather than simply subtracting a flat amount.
40 m³ actually costs 15 + 80 = $95.00, not $85.00.
65.00 × 1.10 = $71.50, applying the same 10% multiplier used to recover May's genuine charge.
solution:
Subtracting cancels x: 7y = 14.00, so y = 2.00. Substituting back: x + 36 = 51, so x = 15.00.
Final Answer: Fixed charge = $15.00  |  Rate = $2.00/m³ (billing office's claim does not match)
general: Uses a percentage-based penalty (division) rather than a flat fee (subtraction), which is a subtly different mechanism from earlier fee-removal tasks and easy to get backwards. Statements A/B both test whether a verbal claim is taken at face value instead of checked against the underlying bills.

title: CityCab vs. MetroX Fare Comparison
format: Text Narrative  |  Difficulty: 3.6/10  |  (previously Task 24 (orig. Tasks 21–30 set))
narrative:
A commuter is deciding between two ride-hailing companies. An 8 km CityCab ride once cost $14.00, and a 20 km CityCab ride cost
exactly $12.00 more than that. Separately, a 5 km MetroX ride cost $13.50, with a 15 km MetroX ride costing exactly $15.00 more.
given:
Each company must be modelled separately. Each "costs $X more than" comparison must first be converted into an absolute fare. Let x1,
y1 be CityCab's base fare and rate, and x2, y2 be MetroX's.
statements: For a 10 km ride, CityCab works out cheaper than MetroX.
Both companies charge the same base fare of $6.00.
For distances under 4 km, MetroX would be cheaper than CityCab.
A 30 km CityCab ride costs $36.00.
There is a distance of 5 km at which both companies charge exactly the same fare.
explanations: At 10 km, CityCab charges $16.00 while MetroX charges $21.00, so CityCab is cheaper.
Both systems independently solve to a $6.00 base fare, a coincidence worth double-checking rather than assuming.
Since both share the same base fare and MetroX's rate is higher, MetroX is never actually cheaper for any positive distance — they only tie at 0 km.
Setting the two fare formulas equal gives d = 0, not 5 km — the companies only match at zero distance.
solution:
For CityCab, subtracting cancels x1: 12y1 = 12, so y1 = 1, x1 = 6. For MetroX: 10y2 = 15, so y2 = 1.5, x2 = 6.
Final Answer: CityCab — base $6.00, rate $1.00/km  |  MetroX — base $6.00, rate $1.50/km
general: Requires solving two entirely independent 2×2 systems (one per company) rather than one, and both are fed by relative "costs $X more" clues that must be converted to absolute fares first. Statements C and E both test the same misconception in different guises: that a lower fixed cost or smaller distance somehow favors the company with the higher rate.

For the upcoming order of 40 units X and 30 units Y, Vendor A is the cheaper overall choice.

explanations: Vendor A's $9 for Product X undercuts Vendor B's $11.

general: Like Task 18, this requires two independent 2×2 systems, but adds a genuine business-decision layer on top: the cheaper-per-unit vendor for one product is not necessarily the cheaper overall vendor for a mixed order. Statement D is the central trap, generalizing from the single-product comparison (B) to the wrong conclusion about the whole order.

title: Alpha & Beta Holdings, Quarterly Dashboard
format: Text Narrative  |  Difficulty: 3.9/10  |  (previously Task 30 (orig. Tasks 21–30 set))
narrative:
Alpha and Beta are sister companies that sell Product P and Service Q at identical market prices. Combined, they earned $27,200 in Q1
revenue, and Beta earned exactly $1,000 more than Alpha. Alpha sold 150 units of P and 80 subscriptions of Q; Beta sold 100 units of P
and 130 subscriptions of Q. (Alpha's headcount grew 8% year-on-year versus Beta's 6% — a staffing detail with no bearing on pricing.)
given:
Individual Q1 revenue figures are not stated directly — only their combined total and the gap between them. Those must first be turned
into Alpha's and Beta's separate revenue figures (a small sum-and-difference step) before the unit-sales data can be used.
statements: Product P is priced at $50 and Service Q at $70, identically for both companies.
Beta generated more Q1 revenue than Alpha.
If Alpha raises Product P's price by 10% next quarter with sales volumes unchanged, its total revenue would increase by exactly 10%.
Alpha's projected revenue after that 10% Product P price increase would surpass Beta's current Q1 revenue.
Beta's revenue from Service Q subscriptions alone exceeds Alpha's entire Q1 revenue from Product P.
explanations: The elimination confirms x = $50 and y = $70, holding for both companies' revenue rows simultaneously.
Beta's $14,100 exceeds Alpha's $13,100 by $1,000, straight out of the Stage 1 sum-and-difference step.
A 10% rise on Product P alone raises Alpha's revenue from $13,100 to $13,850, an increase of only about 5.7%, not 10% — because Product P is only part of Alpha's total revenue.
Alpha's projected revenue of $13,850 still falls short of Beta's current $14,100.
Beta's Service Q revenue is $9,100, while Alpha's entire Product P revenue is $7,500 — Beta's single revenue line from Q alone beats Alpha's whole P line.
solution:
Adding the Stage 1 equations: 2B = 28200, so B = 14100, A = 13100. For Stage 2, dividing by 10 and eliminating gives x = 50, y = 70.
Final Answer: Product P = $50.00  |  Service Q = $70.00
general: The hardest task in this tier: it stacks a preliminary sum-and-difference derivation on top of the usual two-unknown pricing system (a genuine two-stage solve), and its statements C/D test the classic misconception that a percentage change to one revenue stream scales an entire multi- product total by the same percentage.
